core: Probation as a sentence imposed by a court, generally in place of incarceration, and parole as conditional release from prison granted by a paroling authority after part of a sentence has been served

claims.claim: At yearend 2023 an estimated 3,772,000 adults were under community supervision in the United States: 3,103,400 on probation and 680,400 on parole. Over the same period 1,852,900 people were held in prisons or local jails, so roughly twice as many people were under community supervision as were confined.

BJS reports that one in 70 adult U.S. residents was under community supervision during 2023, and that among comparable agencies the total community supervision population fell 23% from yearend 2013 to yearend 2023.

Since the Sentencing Reform Act of 1984 took effect on November 1, 1987, people sentenced to federal prison are no longer eligible for parole and instead serve a term of supervised release after imprisonment. The chapter applies only to offenses committed after that date, so people sentenced for earlier conduct, along with D.C. Code offenders, military prisoners, and people transferred under foreign treaties, remain parole-eligible.

Federal supervised release is imposed by the sentencing judge as part of the sentence under 18 U.S.C. 3583(a) and is served after release from imprisonment; authorized terms run up to five years for a Class A or B felony, three years for a Class C or D felony, and one year for a Class E felony or non-petty misdemeanor. Under 3583(e)(3) a court may revoke supervised release on a preponderance of the evidence and require the person to serve part or all of the term in prison.

Federal probation carries mandatory conditions set by 18 U.S.C. 3563(a) — including not committing another federal, state, or local crime, not unlawfully possessing a controlled substance, submitting to drug testing, making restitution and paying assessments, and notifying the court of material changes in economic circumstances affecting ability to pay — plus discretionary conditions under 3563(b) such as employment, treatment, reporting to a probation officer, residence requirements, and electronic monitoring.

The federal judiciary describes post-conviction supervision officers as working both to protect the community and to assist supervised individuals in making long-term positive changes, using individualized risk assessment to set supervision intensity.

Morrissey v. Brewer, 408 U.S. 471 (1972), decided June 29, 1972, held that parole revocation requires a two-stage process — a prompt preliminary inquiry before a neutral hearing officer near the place of the alleged violation, and a final revocation hearing — and set six minimum requirements: written notice of the claimed violations, disclosure of the evidence, an opportunity to be heard and present evidence, the right to confront and cross-examine adverse witnesses absent a specific good-cause finding, a neutral and detached hearing body, and a written statement of the evidence relied on and the reasons for revoking. The Court said this is not a criminal prosecution and expressly did not decide the right to counsel.

Gagnon v. Scarpelli, 411 U.S. 778 (1973), decided May 14, 1973, extended Morrissey's preliminary and final hearing requirements to probation revocation and held that the right to appointed counsel for an indigent probationer or parolee is decided case by case by the hearing body, with counsel presumptively provided where the person makes a timely and colorable claim of innocence of the violation or raises substantial reasons in justification or mitigation, and with reasons for any refusal stated in the record.

Bearden v. Georgia, 461 U.S. 660 (1983), decided May 24, 1983, held that a sentencing court cannot revoke probation for failure to pay a fine or restitution without evidence and findings that the probationer was responsible for the failure, or that alternative punishments would be inadequate; depriving a probationer of conditional freedom simply because, through no fault of his own, he cannot pay is contrary to the fundamental fairness required by the Fourteenth Amendment.

Among 2023 probation exits with a known exit type, 58.5% were successful completions and 15.9% were exits to incarceration; completion was higher for misdemeanor probation (69.7%) than felony probation (49.5%), and incarceration exits were more than twice as common for felony probation (21.4%) as for misdemeanor probation (9.2%). Among 2023 parole exits with a known type, 63.9% completed and 28.6% returned to incarceration.

In BJS's reported 2023 parole exit data, 73,680 exits were returns to incarceration, of which 47,660 (65%) were returns with revocation rather than with a new sentence — that is, most parole returns to prison that year followed a violation rather than a new criminal sentence.

Of 472,278 admissions of sentenced prisoners to state or federal prison in 2023, 111,385 (24%) were conditional supervision violations — people returned to prison from post-custody community supervision — and 350,628 (74%) were new court commitments. BJS's definition of new court commitments expressly includes probation violators sentenced by a court, so the 24% figure understates the share of prison admissions that begin with a supervision violation. Reporting also varies: Florida, for example, does not report prison admissions for technical violations.

The risk-need-responsivity model was developed in the 1980s and first formalized in 1990 by Andrews, Bonta, and Hoge. Its three core principles are matching supervision and service intensity to assessed risk of reoffending, targeting changeable criminogenic needs rather than non-criminogenic ones, and delivering interventions through cognitive social learning methods adapted to the individual's learning style, motivation, and circumstances.

The American Probation and Parole Association's 2006 caseload standards recommend adult cases-to-staff ratios of 20:1 for intensive supervision, 50:1 for moderate-to-high risk, and 200:1 for low risk, while stressing that caseload (cases assigned) is not the same as workload (time the required tasks generate) and that APPA had previously declined to set fixed numbers because agencies differ so much. These are professional recommendations, not legal requirements.

The NIJ-funded HOPE Demonstration Field Experiment, a four-site randomized controlled trial with 1,504 enrolled probationers in Arkansas, Massachusetts, Oregon, and Texas, found that HOPE-style swift, certain, and fair supervision did not reduce recidivism: 40% of HOPE versus 44% of probation-as-usual participants had a new arrest, 25% versus 22% had a revocation, and 28% versus 26% had a new conviction. HOPE participants were more likely to go to jail (82% versus 56%), served more total jail days (47 versus 33), and cost more. The original Hawaii evaluations had reported much larger benefits.

Financial conditions are a measured compliance problem in supervision: in the HOPE Demonstration Field Experiment, 18% of probation-as-usual participants and 11% of HOPE participants were violated for failing to pay fees and fines. The U.S. Commission on Civil Rights reported in 2017 that nonpayment of legal financial obligations can trigger driver's license suspension in at least eight of the fifteen states with the largest prison populations, and that some states incarcerate people or extend probation or parole for nonpayment.

BJS's Annual Parole Survey counts federal supervised release inside its federal parole figures, which means national parole totals include a population that is legally not parole. BJS states this explicitly in its methodology.

Probation supervision generates very large administrative flows: BJS estimated 1,626,300 entries to and 1,607,500 exits from probation during 2023, and 311,400 entries to and 335,800 exits from parole.

positions: The original Hawaii evaluations (Hawken and Kleiman, 2009, as summarized in the NIJ final report) reported large one-year gains for HOPE participants, including a 33 percentage point reduction in positive drug tests and a 26 percentage point reduction in new arrests.

The NIJ-funded four-site randomized replication found no reduction in arrest, revocation, or reconviction, more jail use, and higher costs; the authors concluded there is little support for expecting substantial improvements over probation as usual when HOPE is implemented widely.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports both, states that the multisite randomized replication is the stronger design, and does not present swift-certain-fair supervision as either proven or discredited. It also notes the report's own caveats: implementation fidelity was good but violation hearings often missed the three-day target, probation-as-usual revocation rates were already low in two sites, and Judge Alm has said the Hawaii model layered swift sanctions on top of an RNR and motivational-interviewing approach that the trial did not test.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What share of prison admissions comes from supervision violations?
positions: BJS's Prisoners series reports that 24% of 2023 admissions were conditional supervision violations, a category limited to returns from post-custody supervision.

Because BJS counts probation violators sentenced by a court as new court commitments, the true share of admissions traceable to a supervision violation is larger than 24%, but BJS's national tables do not isolate it.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson gives the BJS figure with its exact definition and states plainly that it is a floor rather than a total, and that state reporting practice varies. It does not substitute a non-BJS estimate.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is federal supervised release a form of parole?
positions: BJS's Annual Parole Survey counts federal supervised release within its parole category for statistical purposes.

Legally, supervised release is imposed by the sentencing judge under 18 U.S.C. 3583 and is served in addition to a full prison term, whereas parole is a discretionary early release from a prison term granted by a paroling authority.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the legal distinction as the correct one and flags the BJS counting convention as a measurement caveat students will meet in the data.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive claims about probation or parole at all — only placeholder text calling the topic 'a foundational concept' and describing it as a 'label on a toolbox drawer'. None of it was evidence-bearing, and none of it survives.

The draft's implication that the topic is a single concept is wrong: probation and parole are two different legal statuses created by two different decision-makers at two different points, and conflating them is the central error the lesson exists to correct.

sourceRecords.title: Morrissey v. Brewer, 408 U.S. 471 (1972)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government Publishing Office (govinfo), United States Reports
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: The bound-volume PDF was downloaded and the full opinion read. Argued April 11, 1972; decided June 29, 1972. Burger, C.J., delivered the opinion, joined by Stewart, White, Blackmun, Powell, and Rehnquist; Brennan, joined by Marshall, concurred in the result; Douglas dissented in part. Supports the two-stage structure, the six minimum requirements at 489, the statement that revocation is not to be equated with a criminal prosecution and that the process should remain flexible enough to consider evidence inadmissible at trial, and the Court's express refusal to decide whether a parolee is entitled to retained or appointed counsel.

sourceRecords.title: Gagnon v. Scarpelli, 411 U.S. 778 (1973)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government Publishing Office (govinfo), United States Reports
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: The bound-volume PDF was downloaded and the full opinion read. Argued January 9, 1973; decided May 14, 1973. Powell, J., delivered the opinion, joined by Burger, C.J., and Brennan, Stewart, White, Marshall, Blackmun, and Rehnquist; Douglas filed a statement dissenting in part. Supports the extension of Morrissey's preliminary and final hearings to probation revocation, the case-by-case rule for appointed counsel with its presumptive triggers, the requirement that reasons for refusing counsel be stated in the record, and the Court's contrast between a revocation hearing and a criminal trial (no prosecutor, no formal rules of evidence, a hearing body described as predictive and discretionary as well as factfinding).

sourceRecords.title: Bearden v. Georgia, 461 U.S. 660 (1983)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government Publishing Office (govinfo), United States Reports
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: The bound-volume PDF was downloaded and the syllabus and opinion read. Argued January 11, 1983; decided May 24, 1983. O'Connor, J., delivered the opinion, joined by Brennan, Marshall, Blackmun, and Stevens; White, J., concurred in the judgment, joined by Burger, C.J., and Powell and Rehnquist, JJ. sourceRecords.title: Post-Conviction Supervision
sourceRecords.provider: Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts (uscourts.gov)
sourceRecords.notes: Reached through a 301 redirect from /services-forms/probation-and-pretrial-services/probation-and-pretrial-services-supervision. The federal judiciary's own account of post-conviction supervision: probation as an alternative to incarceration, supervised release as supervision following imprisonment for more serious offenses, officers working both to protect the community and to help supervised people make lasting changes, individualized assessment used to set supervision intensity, and universal conditions supplemented by judge-imposed conditions such as curfews, association limits, and treatment. The page carries no statistics. Used to corroborate the dual-role description; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Evaluation of the Honest Opportunity Probation with Enforcement Demonstration Field Experiment (HOPE DFE), Final Report (NCJ 251758)
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Justice / Office of Justice Programs (NCJRS), U.S. Department of Justice
sourceRecords.notes: The full 268-page report was downloaded and the executive summary, findings, and conclusions read. Authors Pamela K. Lattimore, Debbie Dawes (RTI International), Doris L. MacKenzie, and Gary Zajac (Penn State Justice Center for Research); report dated February 2018 under NIJ award 2011-RY-BX-0003; sites were Saline County AR, Essex County MA, Clackamas County OR, and Tarrant County TX. Supports the design (four-site RCT, 1,504 enrolled, 743 HOPE and 761 probation as usual), the null recidivism findings (40% vs 44% rearrest, 25% vs 22% revocation, 28% vs 26% reconviction), the higher jail use (82% vs 56% jailed, 3.8 vs 1.4 stays, 47 vs 33 days) and higher costs, the fee-and-fine violation rates (11% HOPE vs 18% PAU), the summary of the earlier Hawaii results the trial was testing, and the authors' own caveats about probation-as-usual context and untested RNR layering. NCJRS states the report was prepared with federal funds and not published by DOJ; the views are the authors'.

sourceRecords.title: Risk-Need-Responsivity Model for Offender Assessment and Rehabilitation (2007-06)
sourceRecords.notes: Read on Public Safety Canada's own site. Supports the attribution of the risk-need-responsivity model to Andrews, Bonta, and Hoge - developed in the 1980s and first formalized in 1990 - and the definitions of the three principles: match level of service to risk of reoffending; target dynamic criminogenic needs rather than non-criminogenic ones such as self-esteem; and deliver interventions through general responsivity (cognitive social learning methods) and specific responsivity (adapting to learning style, motivation, and personal characteristics). Government of Canada reuse terms were not verified, so no wording was reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Caseload Standards for Probation and Parole (September 2006)
sourceRecords.notes: The 9-page issue paper (primary author Bill Burrell) was downloaded and read. Supports the adult cases-to-staff ratios APPA recommends (intensive 20:1, moderate-to-high risk 50:1, low risk 200:1, administrative with no practical limit), the juvenile ratios, the explicit distinction between caseload and workload, APPA's earlier refusal to set fixed standards because agencies differ so much, and its statement that average caseloads in many jurisdictions are much larger than practitioners would recommend. Presented in the lesson as a professional recommendation, dated 2006, not as a legal requirement. No license is stated on the document; REFERENCE_ONLY and no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Targeted Fines and Fees Against Communities of Color: Civil Rights and Constitutional Implications (September 2017)
sourceRecords.notes: The 238-page statutory enforcement report was downloaded and the relevant passages read. Used narrowly and descriptively for two documented factual points: nonpayment of legal financial obligations can lead to driver's license suspension in at least eight of the fifteen states with the highest prison populations, and some states incarcerate people or extend probation or parole terms for nonpayment. The report also restates the Bearden and Tate ability-to-pay rule, which the lesson takes from the opinions themselves. The Commission's recommendations and its findings about racial targeting are contested policy conclusions and are not used; this lesson takes no policy position.
